events.text: Welcome to the Staffkin Podcast, the show about workplace psychology for people who manage people.
I'm Sam.
Every fact we use is sourced in the description.
Today, psychological safety and workplace conflict.
What the phrase actually means, where it came from, what Google found when it studied its own teams, and what the rules in Canada and here in Nova Scotia expect from an employer.
My guest is Owen.

events.text: Owen plays a manager who has run restaurant and care home teams for twenty years.

events.text: Welcome, Owen.

card.text: Psychological safety isn't comfort. It's being able to speak up.

events.text: And I want to clear something up before we start, because this phrase gets a bad reputation.

card.text: Psychological safety isn't comfort. It's being able to speak up.

events.text: Psychological safety does not mean everyone is comfortable all the time.

events.text: For Halifax this year, it's thirty dollars an hour, up from twenty nine dollars and forty cents last year.
And the minimum wage?
Nova Scotia's minimum wage is seventeen dollars an hour, in effect since October first.

The report says the gap between the living wage and the minimum wage in the province is just under twelve dollars an hour, and that close to half of the Nova Scotia labour market earns less than the living wage.
Northern Nova Scotia went up a lot too, right?
Global News reported it rose almost ten percent, to twenty eight dollars an hour, mostly because of rent.
And to be clear, the living wage is voluntary.

events.text: Fair.
Alright, let's get into it.
Let's start with the definition.
Where does the phrase actually come from?
The version everyone uses comes from a researcher named Amy Edmondson.

card.text: A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking

events.text: In nineteen ninety nine she published a study defining team psychological safety as a shared belief, held by people on a team, that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.

events.text: Asking a question that sounds basic.
Admitting you dropped the ball.
Saying, I think we're doing this wrong.
Asking for help.
Every one of those carries a small social risk.
Psychological safety is the belief that you won't be punished or humiliated for taking it.
And it's a team thing, not a personality thing.

events.text: Asking for feedback, talking about errors, testing assumptions, asking people outside the team for help.
Her measure of safety explained a big share of the differences in learning between teams.
Now, she was honest about the limits.
It was one company and one point in time, so it shows a link, not proof of cause.
Now let's do the myths.
What is it not?

That it means everyone agrees.
A team where nobody ever disagrees isn't safe.
It's quiet.
Disagreement about the work is a sign that people feel free to speak.
And the last one, that it means never feeling uncomfortable.
Right.

events.text: And the error rates across the units varied a lot.

events.text: From about two point three errors per thousand patient days, to about twenty three point seven.

events.text: And when she lined those up against the survey, the units whose people rated their manager and their team most highly had the highest error rates.

events.text: Not the lowest.
Which sounds like a disaster for her theory.
It did.
And here's the bit I love.
Instead of hiding the result, she asked what it meant.
The errors in the study were the errors that got found and recorded.
So the number depends on two things.
How many mistakes people make, and how willing they are to report them.
And you can't tell those apart from the numbers.

events.text: None of these prove anything on their own, but a few together are worth paying attention to.
First sign.
Bad news arrives late.
You find out about the problem on the day it explodes, not the week it started.
Second sign.
In meetings, the same one or two people do all the talking, and everyone else waits to see what the boss thinks before they say anything.
Third?
Your customers find your mistakes before your staff tell you about them.
If a complaint is the first time you hear that the dishwasher has been broken for three days, someone knew, and didn't feel they could say it.
Fourth sign.

People believe what they see you do much more than anything you say in a meeting.

If it's safe to do so, yes.
Set the rules at the start.
One person talks at a time.
We're here to fix how we work, not to decide who's a bad person.
Then let each person say what they need, and look for the part of the work you can change.

One.

events.text: A low number of reported problems can be a warning sign.
In the hospital study, the best led units reported the most errors.
Three.
At Google, how a team worked mattered more than who was on it, and psychological safety topped the list.
Good news for small teams.
Four.
Canada has a voluntary national standard with thirteen factors you can use as a free checklist.
And in Nova Scotia, provincially regulated workplaces need a written harassment prevention policy, with training and no retaliation.
Five.
Go first, ask real questions, thank the messenger, keep the bar high, and deal with whoever makes speaking up risky.
And remember the cold open.
The quiet team isn't always the healthy one.
